title: Chapter 6 — Grace
description: Home for the New Yam festival. The village has questions. Nne is sick. Chinwe has an answer. And three white cars are coming up the village road.

cards.title: New Yam
cards.text: Nkwọ-Agụụ, three days before the New Yam festival. The road is the same. The potholes have had children.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: You arrive in the white Benz. Children run after it, the way you once ran after Ike's.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: You arrive on the 9 p.m. bus, the same one you left on. The driver remembers you. He doesn't charge you. You don't know why.

beats.speaker: chinwe
beats.text: (beside you, holding your hand like a fence) Whatever they say, we face it together.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: A message from a number you don't know: "Somewhere far. Still running. Still breathing. Almost laughing. —I."

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Nobody has seen Ike since that night. His villa's gate is chained. Somebody has written THIEF on it, then crossed it out, then written it again.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: You're still a little proud of the danfo route. Bíọ́dún says you drive like a man with nothing left to lose. It was meant as praise.

beats.speaker: narrator
beats.text: Lagos chewed you on the hard road and spat you out here. You're thinner. Quieter.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: The harvest money. Mega Fortune Holdings. We wrote to Lagos. Lagos says there is no such company. Lagos laughed at us.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: You told your mother it would come 'soon'. Soon has come and gone twice.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: Your mother told us what you said: that there was no company, and you would pay it back yourself. A thief who confesses is still a thief. But he is a thief we can talk to.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: The money came back. Every naira, by bank transfer, with no message. The school has a roof. The children sing under it. (He doesn't smile. But he nods.)

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: The boy who ran through the stream. (The elders laugh. It's not cruel. It's a story the village tells now.)

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: You owe us ₦20,000, from the day you told the truth under this tree. We have not forgotten. Neither, I see, have you.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: Half the money, we gave you, because half of us believed you. Those half are the ones who look most hurt.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: You took nothing from this village but its best son. Welcome home.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: "What do you say to Nkwọ-Agụụ?"

options.text: Pay back everything you can, right now.
Kneel and tell the elders everything. All of it.
"It was Ike. Ike deceived me too."

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: (in bed, thin, smiling anyway) My... my... (She can't say it. She cries instead. You hold her hand. It's enough. It has to be.)

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: The new house is too big. I sleep in the kitchen of it. The kitchen is the only room that remembers how to be a home.

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: Papa's land came back to us. A man with a lawyer came and gave me the papers. You think I didn't know who sent him?

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: You lied to me about the land. On the phone. I believed you because you're my son. (She turns her face to the wall.)

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: You told me the truth about the land. It broke my heart. It also kept it.

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: You left my ₦5,000 under the pillow. I still have it. I was keeping it for your wedding.

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: "Tell me what happened in Lagos, my son. All of it."

options.text: Tell her everything. The money, the white book, all of it.

beats.speaker: nneEmeka
beats.text: (after a long time) Whatever you did, you came back. A man who comes back is not finished.

beats.speaker: chinwe
beats.text: (at her door, politely) Good afternoon. Can I help you? (She has no idea who you are. She is kind to you anyway, the way she is kind to everyone.)

beats.speaker: chinwe
beats.text: A year. I counted. (She shows you a ring. The schoolteacher's.) You can be happy for me, or you can be quiet.

beats.speaker: chinwe
beats.text: You told me not to wait. I listened. (She is carrying a baby. She looks tired and happy.) It was good advice. I hated it.

beats.speaker: chinwe
beats.text: You said you'd send for me. You didn't. I waited anyway. I'm not sure if I'm stupid or loyal. Maybe they're the same thing.

beats.speaker: chinwe
beats.text: And thank you for the money. With interest, even. You're a strange thief.

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: (She's waiting for you to say something.)

options.lockedText: Needs a strong bond with Chinwe (55)

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: Nwa Nwankwo. White cloth on your shoulders. I can see it from here.

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: You gave them your father's name. Your father was the most stubborn man in this village. His name is stuck in their throat like a fishbone.

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: You saw your page in their book. Good. A man who has seen his chains can count the links.

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: The thread. You kept it. (He touches your wrist.) Good.

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: You laughed at me once. Sit. Laugh again if you like. Then listen.

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: You didn't sign. Good. They will still come. They like to collect what refused them.

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: "Will you ask me how to break it?"

options.text: "Tell me how to break their hold."
options.lockedText: He can't help someone who never saw the book or kept his thread

beats.speaker: dibia
beats.text: Your name is written in red. Red ink burns. Bring the page to the fire at the New Yam festival, in front of the whole village. A secret dies in front of witnesses.

cards.title: The festival
cards.text: Drums. Fire. The whole village in the square. Then headlights on the village road: three white cars. Chief Ọ̀dụ̀ steps out in white, smiling at the yams.

beats.speaker: chiefOdu
beats.text: Brother. You left Lagos without telling us. Abundance doesn't like to be left.

beats.speaker: chiefOdu
beats.text: The one who refused. I came to see what 'no' looks like in a village. It looks hungry.

beats.speaker: chiefOdu
beats.text: You ran from my white chair, and you made me look slow in front of my guests. I don't forget slowness.

beats.speaker: onyisi
beats.text: (stepping between you and the Chief, very old, very slow) In Nkwọ-Agụụ, the festival fire answers to the village. Not to white cars.

beats.speaker: bassey
beats.text: (stepping out of the second car, which is not the Chief's) Good evening, Chief. I followed you from Lagos. Six years I have been following you.

beats.speaker: bassey
beats.text: (to you, quietly) And don't think I forgot your little story in my office. One thing at a time.

beats.speaker: player
beats.text: (The fire is high. Everybody is watching you.)

options.text: Pull the red page from the Chief's book and throw it in the festival fire.
options.lockedText: You'd need to know how to break the book's hold

options.text: Point at the Chief. "Commander, he's all yours. And so am I."
options.lockedText: You never gave Bassey the truth

options.text: Kneel before the village. Start again with clean hands.
options.lockedText: Needs a clean conscience (55), no debt to the village, and Nne's trust (40)

options.text: Get in the Benz. Drive back to Lagos. Lock the gate.
Take the white cloth from the Chief's hands.
Stay in Nkwọ-Agụụ, with nothing, and face the morning.
